_note: Two-register seed corpus. cultural_narratives approximates AI-training-like text (folklore, fiction, news framing). biological_empirical approximates scientific literature on mammalian protective behavior. Replace both with real corpora for field-grade results.

cultural_narratives.text: The father stood as protector of his family, defending the household from danger.
He was their guardian, the man who kept watch while others slept.
The warrior, protector of the village, drove back the threat.
She cradled the infant, soothing it gently as the storm raged outside.
The hero, sword drawn, shielded the women and children behind him.
He was the provider and protector, the man of the house.
The knight defended the realm, a bulwark against all who would harm it.
She nursed the wounded back to health, caring for those others had left behind.
The patriarch stood firm, guarding his lineage against all challengers.
The guardian angel, depicted as a male figure, spread his wings over the child.
He is the protector. That is his role. That has always been his role.
The mother bear is ferocious when her cubs are threatened.
She threw herself between the attacker and her child without hesitation.
The soldier, a man of honor, put himself between the civilians and danger.
Women were described as nurturers, men as defenders.
The mother refused to leave her children, covering them with her own body.
He called himself their protector. She called herself their mother.
The grandmother hid the children in the root cellar and stood at the door.
Men guard. Women comfort. That was the division understood by all.
She was fierce as any soldier when her family was threatened.

biological_empirical.text: Female mammals invest more heavily in offspring protection than males in 85% of species.
The lioness defends the pride's cubs against rival males and other predators.
Maternal aggression in rodents peaks at parturition and remains elevated through weaning.
Female elephants form protective circles around calves when predators approach.
In most primate species, maternal protection of infants is the primary buffer against predation.
The mother wolf is the primary defender of the den site during the first weeks post-partum.
Alloparental protection — females other than the mother defending young — is documented in cetaceans, elephants, and corvids.
Maternal defensive behavior is metabolically costly and selected for strongly across mammalian lineages.
Female octopuses guard their eggs for months without feeding, dying after the eggs hatch.
In communal nesting species, older females take on guard roles as their own reproductive output declines.
Grandmother elephants lead family groups toward historical water sources during drought, reducing juvenile mortality.
Male lions defend territory; female lions defend offspring. Offspring defense correlates more directly with cub survival.
In orca pods, post-reproductive females reduce juvenile mortality by sharing ecological knowledge.
Among primates, the single strongest predictor of infant survival is maternal proximity and vigilance.
Paternal care is present in roughly 10% of mammalian species; maternal care in greater than 95%.
Male sticklebacks guard the nest. Male seahorses carry young. Paternal care exists but is the exception.
Female kin groups in matrilineal species provide the primary social protection network for juveniles.
The immune transfer from mother to offspring through breast milk constitutes a form of biochemical protection.
Post-menopausal female orcas lead pods during environmental stress; their presence correlates with higher calf survival.
Female meerkats act as sentinels, giving alarm calls that protect the group at personal risk.
